title: Network basics
desc: LAN, IP, DHCP, DNS, VLAN and cables in plain words

pages.h: A LAN is your own local network
pages.t: A LAN connects computers, printers and phones inside a limited area, like one office, a home or a building. The equipment is managed locally. Most LANs use two technologies: Ethernet cables and Wi-Fi.
g: Local Area Network: the network inside one building or site.
The standard wired network technology, with cables ending in RJ45 plugs.

pages.t: A WAN covers a much bigger area and usually runs over leased lines or internet links. A company that links its offices in Helsinki and Copenhagen is building a WAN. The LAN is the room, the WAN is the road between rooms.
g: Wide Area Network: connects sites far apart, often via the internet or leased lines.

pages.t: The internet is a global system of connected networks. Your LAN reaches it through a router and a provider (ISP). So a typical customer has a LAN inside, a WAN link out, and the internet beyond.
g: Internet Service Provider: the company that sells the internet connection.

quiz.q: What best describes a LAN?
o: A network inside a limited area such as an office
quiz.w: A LAN covers a limited area like a home, office or building and is managed locally.

quiz.q: A customer links offices in two cities over the internet. What is that link?
quiz.w: Links across long distances between sites are WAN links.

quiz.q: What are the two most common LAN technologies?
quiz.w: Wired Ethernet and wireless Wi-Fi are the two most common LAN technologies.

pages.t: An IP address is like a postal address for a device on a network. Data needs to know where to go and where it came from. Every phone, laptop, camera and access point on a network gets one.
g: A number that identifies a device on a network so data can find it.

pages.t: A public address is reachable on the internet, and the router often gets one from the ISP. Inside the LAN, devices use private addresses that are not usable directly on the internet. Many different LANs can reuse the same private ranges.
g: An address used only inside a local network, reserved by a standard (RFC 1918).

pages.t: IPv4 has about 4.3 billion addresses, and the free supply has run out. IPv6 uses much longer addresses (128 bits instead of 32), giving a huge supply. They are not directly compatible, so many networks run both side by side.
g: The newer address system with a practically unlimited supply of addresses.

quiz.q: Why was IPv6 created?
quiz.w: IPv4 only has about 4.3 billion addresses, which was not enough.
g: The older address system with about 4.3 billion addresses.

quiz.q: Which address would a laptop normally have inside an office LAN?
quiz.w: Devices inside a LAN normally use private addresses; the router holds the public one.

quiz.q: Are IPv4 and IPv6 directly compatible?
o: No, so networks often run both
quiz.w: They are not backwards compatible, so running both (dual stack) is the easiest path.

pages.t: When a device joins a network, DHCP gives it an IP address automatically, plus other settings like the gateway and DNS server. Nobody has to type numbers into each device. Many routers have a DHCP server built in.
g: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol: gives devices their network settings automatically.
The router address a device sends traffic to when the destination is outside the LAN.

pages.t: DHCP addresses are lent for a set time, called a lease. Devices renew it while they stay. If a device leaves, the address returns to the pool. Two DHCP servers on one network can cause confusing conflicts.
g: The time a device may keep an address given by DHCP.

pages.t: People type names like a website address, computers need IP numbers. DNS translates one into the other, like a phone book. When websites fail but pinging a raw IP number still works, a DNS problem is a common suspect.
g: Domain Name System: turns names into IP addresses.

quiz.q: What does DHCP do?
quiz.w: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses and settings to devices.
g: Gives devices their network settings automatically.

quiz.q: What does DNS do?
quiz.w: DNS works like a phone book: names in, IP addresses out.

quiz.q: Where does a small office usually get DHCP from?
quiz.w: Many routers include a DHCP server that hands out private addresses to the LAN.

pages.t: A router connects different networks and forwards traffic between them, for example your LAN and the internet. The default route (default gateway) handles everything that is not local. It is the doorway out of the building.
g: Device that forwards data between networks.

pages.t: A switch connects devices inside one LAN with cables. It learns which device sits on which port and sends data only where needed. More ports mean more wired devices, like PCs, phones and cameras.
g: Device with many ports that connects wired devices in a LAN.

pages.t: An access point (AP) gives Wi-Fi to a wired network. A home wireless router combines router, switch and AP in one box. Businesses often split them up so each part can be chosen and placed right.
g: Device that connects Wi-Fi devices to the wired network.
A home box combining router, switch, Wi-Fi and sometimes modem.

quiz.q: Which device connects your LAN to the internet?
quiz.w: The router forwards traffic between networks, such as LAN and internet.

quiz.q: A shop wants ten wired cash registers and printers on one network. What is the key device?
quiz.w: A switch connects many wired devices in the same LAN.

quiz.q: What is a home wireless router?
o: Router, switch and AP in one box
quiz.w: Home units combine routing, switching and Wi-Fi in a single device.

src.l: Wikipedia: List of TCP and UDP port numbers

pages.t: NAT rewrites addresses as traffic leaves the router, so a whole office of private addresses can share one public address. It helped IPv4 last longer. By default, connections can only be started from inside.
g: Network Address Translation: lets many private devices share one public address.

pages.t: Because outside connections are blocked by default, a camera or server inside needs a port forward to be reachable from the internet. It sends traffic arriving at a chosen port to one inside device. Use it carefully, since it opens a door.
g: A rule that sends incoming traffic on a given port to a chosen inside device.

pages.t: A protocol is an agreed way of talking. A port is a numbered door for a service. Web pages use port 443 (HTTPS), plain web 80, email between servers 25, and DNS 53. Firewalls often allow or block by port.
g: A set of agreed rules for how devices exchange data.
A number that tells a device which service should receive the data.
The secure version of web traffic.

quiz.q: What does NAT let an office do?
o: Share one public address among many private devices
quiz.w: NAT translates between private addresses and a public one.

quiz.q: A customer wants to view their camera from home over the internet. What does a basic router setup need?
o: A port forward to the camera
quiz.w: NAT blocks outside connections by default, so a forward is needed, with care for security.

quiz.q: Which port is normally used for secure web pages (HTTPS)?
quiz.w: HTTPS uses port 443; 53 is DNS and 25 is email between servers.

pages.t: Bandwidth is how much data a connection can carry per second, like how wide a motorway is. Bigger bandwidth helps with big downloads, many users at once and video streams.
g: The amount of data a link can carry per second.
Megabits per second, the usual unit for internet speed.

pages.t: Latency is the time delay before data arrives, like how long the drive takes. A wide road does not make the trip shorter. Video calls, remote desktop and gaming feel bad when latency is high.
g: Time delay between sending something and it arriving.

pages.t: A customer saying "it is slow" could mean low bandwidth, high latency, or a Wi-Fi problem. Ask what feels slow: downloads, or calls and remote work. The answer points to different fixes.

quiz.q: Which analogy fits latency?
quiz.w: Latency is the delay, like travel time, not the capacity.

quiz.q: A customer's video calls stutter although the speed test shows plenty of bandwidth. What might be an issue?
quiz.w: Real-time traffic suffers from delay even when there is a lot of capacity.

quiz.q: Bigger bandwidth most clearly helps with...
o: Shortening the delay of a single click
Many users and big downloads at once
quiz.w: Bandwidth is capacity, so it helps when lots of data or users share the link.

pages.t: Office cables are twisted-pair copper with RJ45 plugs, normally good for 100 metres. Cat6 is backward compatible with Cat5e. For 10 Gbit/s over the full 100 m, you need Cat6a; Cat6 only manages about 55 m.
g: Grades of copper network cable. Higher grades cope with higher speeds over distance.
The plug on a normal network cable.

pages.t: Fibre carries light, loses little signal and ignores electrical interference. Multi-mode suits short runs inside buildings. Single-mode is for longer links, typically beyond about a kilometre, and between buildings or sites.
g: Fibre with a thin core for long distances.
Fibre with a wider core for short distances.

pages.t: An SFP is a small plug-in module that fits a switch port and matches the cable: fibre or copper. SFP+ is the faster version, known for 10 Gbit/s. Customers can pick the right module for the distance.
g: Hot-swappable transceiver modules; SFP is typically 1 Gbit/s, SFP+ 10 Gbit/s.
A faster port that links a switch to the rest of the network.

quiz.q: Which copper cable is needed for 10 Gbit/s over a full 100 m run?
quiz.w: Cat6a allows 10GBASE-T over 100 m; Cat6 only about 55 m.
g: A higher grade copper cable for 10 Gbit/s over 100 m.

quiz.q: A customer needs a link between two buildings 5 km apart. What fits best?
quiz.w: Single-mode fibre is used for longer links, far beyond what copper can do.

quiz.q: What is an SFP?
o: A swappable transceiver module for a switch port
quiz.w: SFPs are hot-swappable modules matched to fibre or copper cabling.

quiz.q: Why choose fibre over copper between floors with heavy electrical machinery?
o: It is immune to electromagnetic interference
quiz.w: Fibre is immune to electromagnetic interference and loses less signal.

pages.t: A VLAN splits one physical network into separate logical ones. Staff, guests and cameras can share the same cables and switches but stay apart. Membership is set in software, so no rewiring.
g: Virtual LAN: a logical network inside shared physical equipment.

pages.t: VLANs cut unnecessary broadcast traffic and limit who can reach what. A guest on the Wi-Fi should not see the finance server. Careful setup matters: VLANs are not a complete security solution and can be defeated if badly set up.
g: Dividing a network into smaller separated parts.

pages.t: Switches do not pass traffic between VLANs by themselves. A router or Layer 3 switch moves it, and that is also where rules can allow or block. VLAN-capable gear means managed or smart switches.
g: The level where IP addresses and routing work.
One link that carries several VLANs at once.

quiz.q: What is the main idea of a VLAN?
o: Separate logical networks on shared hardware
quiz.w: VLANs keep groups of devices logically isolated on the same cabling.

quiz.q: A hotel wants guest Wi-Fi apart from its booking system on the same switches. What is the concept to use?
quiz.w: VLANs separate guest and internal traffic without extra cabling.

quiz.q: How does traffic get from one VLAN to another?
o: Through a router or Layer 3 device
quiz.w: Switches do not bridge VLANs; a Layer 3 device moves the traffic between them.

pages.t: A small office needs an internet link, a router or firewall at the door, a switch for wired devices and phones, and access points for Wi-Fi. DHCP and DNS usually come from the router.
g: A device that filters traffic between networks by rules.

pages.t: How many users and devices? Any cameras or phones that need PoE? Guest Wi-Fi? Offices to link or remote workers? Fibre or copper in the walls? Answers decide the gear.
g: Power over Ethernet: power through the network cable.

pages.t: Reselling a single home router to a company with guests, cameras and calls. Forgetting PoE budget, or uplink ports for fibre. Not planning VLANs for guests. A short checklist avoids returns and angry customers.

quiz.q: A dentist office has 12 PCs, 6 IP phones and 3 Wi-Fi access points. Which wired device is certainly needed?
quiz.w: A switch connects the wired devices and access points inside the LAN.

quiz.q: Which of these is a key question when choosing the switch?
quiz.w: Phones and access points are often powered over the cable, which sets the PoE need.

quiz.q: A company wants guests kept apart from staff. What do you mention?
o: Plan VLANs and a separate guest Wi-Fi
quiz.w: VLANs plus a guest network separate guests from internal systems.
